transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, Doc. Yeah, thanks for seeing me. I, uh, I guess I'm here because things at work are just... they're getting really out of hand. I'm a construction manager, and I've been doing this a long time, worked my way up right out of high school, so I know the job inside and out. There are always a million moving parts on a site, which I'm used to, but lately... 

What brings me in is, well, take a safety briefing, for example. Or when we sit down in the trailer for a major plan review. I'll go in telling myself, "Alright, you really need to lock in here, this is important." I'll be trying *so* hard to just pay attention to the guy talking or the blueprints sitting right there on the table. But man, I swear, within just a couple of minutes, my mind is completely gone. It's just off on, like, three other job problems at once. 

I'll be sitting there, nodding, staring right at the safety officer, but in my head, I'm stressing about whether the concrete trucks are gonna get backed up at the gate, or if the framing guys have enough material for the afternoon, or some permit issue from last week. And then I kind of snap back to reality and realize the meeting's moving on and I completely missed things. Important things I *know* I should have caught, things it's my actual job to catch. It's just... it's happening all the time now, and it's incredibly frustrating because I can't seem to stop it no matter how hard I try to just sit there and listen.

When you think back over your whole life—say, school, earlier jobs, even just managing things at home—have you always struggled with focus and attention like this, or is this something that's really gotten worse just recently?

Man, you know... I wish I could say this was just the stress of the current job, or that I'm just getting older, because then maybe I could just take a vacation and it would all go away, right? But if I'm being completely honest with you, and really looking back over everything... it's always been like this. It really has. 

I mean, going way, way back, all the way to elementary school. I can still picture the look on my mom's face when she'd come home from those parent-teacher conferences. It was like clockwork every single year. The teachers—I remember Mrs. Davis in third grade, Mr. Henderson in fourth, it really didn't matter who it was—they were already telling my parents back then that I was, well, a handful. They’d sit my folks down and give them this whole spiel about how I just could not, for the life of me, stay in my seat. Like, I’d always find an excuse to get up, go sharpen a pencil, look out the window, check the hallway, whatever. 

And the talking... oh man, I was always getting in trouble because I talked out of turn. The teacher would ask a question and I’d just blurt out the answer before they even finished the sentence, or I'd just be chatting with the kid next to me while she was in the middle of a lesson. 

And it wasn't just that stuff, either. My backpack was an absolute black hole. I lost my homework constantly. My mom used to get so incredibly frustrated because she'd literally sit there and watch me do the math sheet at the kitchen table, and then somehow, between the front door and my desk at school, it would just vanish. And whenever we had classwork, I’d just fly through it. I’d rush through the directions so fast, just skimming the words, that I’d end up doing the whole assignment completely wrong because I didn't actually take the time to understand what they were asking me to do in the first place. I just wanted to get to the end of it, you know? 

So, yeah... long story short, I guess it’s definitely not new. It's just that back then, the stakes were a missing spelling worksheet or a timeout, and now the stakes are a multi-million dollar commercial build and a crew of fifty guys relying on me.

latest_inference.note: Lifelong history of inattention, impulsivity, hyperactivity (inability to stay seated, talking out of turn), and executive dysfunction (losing homework, rushing through instructions) dating back to elementary school, now manifesting as occupational impairment. This strongly supports ADHD, Combined Type. F98.8, F41.1, F32.9, and F06.8 ruled out as they do not explain the decades-long developmental pattern of core ADHD symptoms.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with lifelong history of inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity symptoms beginning in elementary school (age 7-8) and persisting into adulthood. Core ADHD symptoms include: inability to sustain attention in meetings despite effort, mind wandering to multiple competing tasks, difficulty following directions (rushing through instructions), excessive talking/blurting out answers, inability to organize materials (lost homework), and restlessness (inability to remain seated). Symptoms have caused functional impairment across childhood (academic underperformance, teacher reports) and currently in occupational setting (missing critical work information, performance concerns). No evidence of other primary psychiatric or medical conditions better explaining the presentation. F90.9 (Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, unspecified) is appropriate given the clear adult ADHD presentation with childhood onset.
